opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a pretty poor model of human memory, even though it's an extremely effective engineering solution.

If you look at what long context really is, it's essentially keeping everything: every token you've ever seen in the current episode sits there in the KV cache, uncompressed, and at each step the model can attend back to any of it with full fidelity. That's closer to a perfect tape recorder than to memory. Human memory doesn't work like that at all. We forget most of what we experience. What we keep is heavily compressed, abstracted, reorganized, and often reconstructed when we recall it, sometimes incorrectly. And I don't think that's a bug. The forgetting and compression are where a lot of the intelligence comes from, because to compress you have to figure out what matters, what the structure is, what can be thrown away.

There's also a cost issue that tells you something. With attention, the cost grows with context length, quadratically in the vanilla form, and even with all the tricks, memory grows linearly with how much you've seen. A person living for decades is processing an enormous stream of input, and there's no way the brain is storing it as a growing raw buffer and searching it every time. So structurally the brain must be doing something more like a recurrent state that gets continuously updated, plus some slower consolidation process that writes important things into long-term storage, into the weights, so to speak.

So the way I'd frame it is that current models have two extremes. One is the parameters, which are learned slowly through training and very compressed. The other is the context, which is fast but uncompressed and expensive. What's missing is the middle layer, something that can take experience from the context and gradually distill it into a compact, persistent form, a bit like what sleep and consolidation do for us. Without that, the model doesn't really learn from its own experience at deployment time; it just reads a longer and longer transcript.

That's also why I'm somewhat skeptical of the idea that simply pushing context to millions or tens of millions of tokens solves the memory problem or the continual learning problem. It helps a lot for practical tasks like reading a codebase or a long document. But if we want systems that accumulate experience over long periods, like a person who gets better at their job over years, I think we need architectures that compress, that are allowed to forget, and that can turn short-term memory into long-term knowledge. Linear attention, state-space models, and various memory mechanisms are early attempts in that direction, but I don't think anyone has found the right answer yet. It's one of the more important open problems.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformer context keeps every token uncompressed in the KV cache and contrasts this with memory that compresses and abstracts information.

r002.rationale: It says people retain what matters, but does not state that retention is guided by likely future usefulness.

r003.rationale: It discusses a missing middle layer but does not identify intermediate-term human memory as allowing someone to resume work without rereading the source material.

r004.rationale: It compares slow, compressed parameters to long-term storage and says important experience could be written into weights, “so to speak.”

r005.rationale: The response contrasts fast context with slow parameters and discusses short-term memory, but does not clearly equate Transformer context specifically with only the short-term component of human memory.

r006.rationale: It says expanding context to millions of tokens does not solve the memory or continual-learning problem, and that models still do not learn from deployment experience.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think the long context of a Transformer is really memory in the human sense. What a Transformer does with a long context is more like keeping everything laid out on the table in front of you. Every token is still there, you can attend back to any of it, nothing has been compressed or forgotten. That is actually the opposite of how human memory works. Human memory is lossy on purpose. We throw away almost everything and keep a compressed representation, and the compression is where the intelligence lives, because deciding what to keep is itself a judgment about what matters.

So when people say "the context window is the model's memory," I think that is a bit misleading. The context is more like a very large working memory, or even just perception. The thing that actually behaves like memory in a Transformer is the weights. The weights are what the model has distilled from everything it has seen, and that distillation is irreversible, just like ours. The problem is that in today's systems this layer is frozen after training. The model cannot keep writing to it during use. So you end up with a strange split: a huge, perfect, short-term buffer on one side, and a long-term store that never updates on the other. Humans have neither of those. Our short-term buffer is tiny and our long-term store is constantly being rewritten.

There is also a cost argument that I think points in the same direction. Attention cost grows with context length, and that is not an engineering accident, it is the price of refusing to forget. Biology clearly decided that price was not worth paying. If you look at it from the perspective of what an efficient system should do, a model that reads a million tokens and treats them all as equally available is wasting most of that computation. The more interesting question is how you build something in between: a model that can compress its history into state, decide what deserves to be retained, and then retrieve from that compressed state when it needs to. Linear attention, state-space models, RNN-style recurrence, these are all attempts at that, and none of them have fully solved it yet, because compression means loss and you have to be smart about which losses are acceptable.

So my honest assessment is that long context is a very useful engineering tool, but as a model of human memory it is mostly a counterexample. It shows you what memory would look like if you had unlimited storage and no need to forget. Studying where it breaks down, where the model gets lost in the middle of a long input, or can't tell what was important, actually tells you more about why forgetting is a feature than about how to replicate recall.

r001.rationale: The response says standard Transformer context leaves every token available and that “nothing has been compressed or forgotten,” contrasting this with lossy human memory.

r002.rationale: It says human memory keeps what matters, but does not state that it preferentially retains information likely to be useful in the future.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe an intermediate-term memory that lets people continue prior work without rereading the original material.

r004.rationale: It identifies Transformer weights as memory, saying they contain what the model has distilled from experience, analogous to irreversible human memory.

r005.rationale: It compares context to a large working memory or perception and describes it as a huge short-term buffer.

r006.rationale: It explains that a million-token context treating everything as equally available wastes computation and that models can still lose track of important information in long inputs.

astra-6.text:
I think long context captures one aspect of human memory: information from earlier can influence what we do now. But I’d be cautious about treating it as a complete model of memory.

A Transformer can attend to information that remains in its context. Human memory often works under a different condition: the original experience is no longer available, and we have to reconstruct something useful from it. We forget details, retain patterns, and sometimes change our recollection as we acquire new information. So the question isn’t just how much you can keep accessible. It’s what you preserve, how you retrieve it, and how it shapes future learning.

For example, you might remember the lesson of a conversation without remembering any of its exact sentences. A longer context gives a model more of the conversation to work with, but that alone doesn’t establish that it has formed that kind of lasting memory.

So I see long context as a useful component—perhaps closer to an accessible workspace—but not the whole story. A fuller account would also need to explain selective retention, consolidation, and retrieval when the original context is gone.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human forgetting and pattern retention with information available in context, but does not identify the absence of compression in standard Transformer context.

r002.rationale: It says people retain patterns, but does not state that memory preferentially keeps information likely to be useful in the future.

r003.rationale: It does not describe intermediate-term memory or continuing previous work without rereading the original material.

r004.rationale: It does not compare enduring human memories to information stored in neural-network parameters.

r005.rationale: It calls long context an accessible workspace and a component of memory, but does not characterize Transformer context as analogous specifically to short-term memory.

r006.rationale: The response says longer context alone does not establish lasting memory, but does not clearly state that greater capacity fails to solve the problem of using contextual information effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long context captures one aspect of human memory: earlier information can remain available and influence what we do next. But having access to a long history is different from remembering it the way a person does.

Human memory is selective and reconstructive. We don’t keep a complete transcript of our lives. We retain some details, compress others into general knowledge, and retrieve different things depending on our current situation. Sometimes we also remember incorrectly.

A Transformer with a long context window can look back at a large amount of information, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned what to preserve over time. So I’d treat long context as a useful component of a memory system, rather than a complete model of human memory. The interesting question is how it interacts with learning, compression, and retrieval—how an experience changes what the system knows, even after that experience leaves the context window.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformers may not learn what to preserve and mentions compression, but does not clearly identify the absence of compression in standard Transformer context as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It describes human memory as selective and situation-dependent, but does not say it preferentially retains information likely to be useful in the future.

r003.rationale: It does not describe an intermediate-term memory that lets people continue prior work without rereading the source material.

r004.rationale: It does not compare enduring human memories to information solidified in neural network parameters.

r005.rationale: It calls long context a useful component of memory, but does not characterize traditional Transformer context as only the short-term component of human memory.

r006.rationale: It says a long context window provides access to a large history but does not necessarily mean the Transformer has learned what to preserve over time, conveying that more context capacity alone does not ensure effective use of that information.
